Let me analyze these teaching examples carefully to identify systematic errors in the forecasts compared to true outcomes.

Looking at the examples, they all appear to be centered around EU ETS (carbon) prices around the 70-75 EUR/MT range in August 2024, and earlier in June 2024.

Let me examine the patterns:

## Example 1 (2024-08-23)
- History: Prices have been declining from ~73.14 down to ~71.57 over the last 18 days
- Model forecasts: Start around 71.40-71.84, gradually declining to ~69-70 by day 17-30
- True outcomes: Start around 71.13, declining more sharply to ~62-63 by day 30

The model is too high! It under-forecasts the decline.

## Example 2 (2024-08-22)
- Nearly identical to Example 1, with the same error pattern
- Model forecasts are ~1-3 euros too high
- True outcomes are 1-3 euros too low

## Example 3 (2024-08-21)
- Same pattern - model forecasts are slightly too high
- Differences are consistent with what I see in Examples 1 and 2

## Example 4 (2024-08-20)
- Same pattern

## Example 5 (2024-06-24)
- History: Prices have been declining from ~73.95 down to ~68.05 over the last 18 days
- Model forecasts: Start around 67.82, declining to ~67-68 range
- True outcomes: Start around 67.56, declining more sharply to ~66-67 range

Wait, let me look more carefully. In Example 5, the model starts at 67.82 on day 1, and true outcomes start at 67.56. The differences are about 0.25-0.30 on average initially, then the divergence grows to about 1-2 euros by day 30.
 
I notice a consistent under-forecasting pattern where the model misses the full extent of price declines. The discrepancies appear to grow over time, suggesting the model struggles to capture the full magnitude of price movements. Sentiment doesn't seem to fundamentally alter these underlying forecast deviations.
